what_happened: The spacecraft reached Mars about 170 kilometers lower than planned and was lost. A ground software file sent thruster data to the navigation team in pound force seconds when the agreed unit was newton seconds.
root_cause: A ground software file gave thruster impulse in English units while the interface document required metric units, and the process did not catch it.
what_nasa_did: NASA convened a Mishap Investigation Board that named the units error as the root cause and also found that navigation and systems engineering checks had failed. The lessons learned entry directs teams to verify consistent engineering units on all parameters.
lesson: Check units and conventions at every interface between teams, and test the real data end to end.
design_trigger: Unit conventions are not checked between teams that exchange navigation or thruster data.

sources.title: NASA LLIS 0740 (GlobalSpec mirror of the lesson)
Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report (NASA LLIS library)
IEEE Spectrum: Why the Mars Probe Went Off Course

what_happened: The lander was lost during its landing on Mars. The most probable cause is that it shut down its descent engines too early because it believed it had touched down.
root_cause: Touchdown sensors gave a false signal when the legs deployed, and the flight software did not reliably ignore it.
what_nasa_did: A review team led by Thomas Young concluded that the most probable cause was a premature engine shutdown from spurious leg sensor signals and blamed inadequate software design and systems testing. NASA recorded lessons including repeating the leg deployment test after wiring was corrected.
lesson: Make landing logic immune to known sensor noise and repeat a test after any wiring fix.
design_trigger: Engine cutoff depends on a single touchdown sensor type with no filtering or cross check.

sources.title: Testimony of Thomas Young, Mars Program Independent Assessment Team (SpaceRef)

what_happened: The Genesis sample capsule came back from space but its parachute never opened, and it hit the Utah test range. The sensors that should have told it that it was entering the atmosphere could not feel the slowing down.
root_cause: The deceleration switches were installed in an inverted orientation because of a design error that reviews did not catch.
what_nasa_did: A Mishap Investigation Board found the design error and a weak review process. NASA used the lessons in training and project reviews, and the Stardust capsule used the same parachute concept successfully in 2006.
lesson: Fully test any reused design in its new setup, because redundancy does not help when every copy is wrong the same way.
design_trigger: Redundant sensors that all share one wiring or mounting assumption that was never tested end to end.

what_happened: Galileo's large umbrella style antenna was supposed to open on the way to Jupiter, but it never reached the fully open position. Some of its ribs stayed stuck.
root_cause: Dry film lubricant on a few rib pins was probably worn away during long truck trips and storage, so the ribs stuck.
what_nasa_did: NASA labs built a stuck ribs model and ran friction and wear tests on the lubricant to try to free the antenna. JPL analysis found four of the 18 ribs were affected.
lesson: One shot deployables with no backup need preloaded mechanisms, robust lubrication and a fault tolerant design.
design_trigger: Single deployable antenna with no backup, stored and transported for years before launch.

what_happened: Kepler lost one reaction wheel in July 2012 and a second in May 2013. With only two wheels it could no longer hold steady on its original star field.
root_cause: Reaction wheels wore out and a second failure left too few wheels for three axis pointing.
what_nasa_did: Engineers used sunlight pressure on the solar arrays as a stand in for the lost wheel, so the two remaining wheels could hold the telescope along the ecliptic. NASA approved this new mission, called K2, in May 2014.
lesson: Give pointing systems spare capacity and think about a backup way to steer, such as sunlight pressure.
design_trigger: Pointing system with only the minimum number of reaction wheels and no plan for wheel loss.

sources.title: NASA Exoplanet Exploration Program newsletter: K2 update
That's How We Roll: The NASA K2 Mission (arXiv)

what_happened: Dawn lost its first reaction wheel in June 2010 and a third in April 2017, after losing a second earlier. It had to point itself with thrusters and hydrazine, which ran out in late October 2018.
root_cause: Three of four reaction wheels failed, so pointing and momentum control shifted to thrusters that burn a limited fuel supply.
what_nasa_did: Engineers switched attitude control to the hydrazine thrusters and used them to manage wheel momentum. The mission ended when fuel ran out and the craft was left in a silent orbit around Ceres.
lesson: Fuel is the backup for failed wheels, so size it with margin for losing pointing hardware.
design_trigger: Attitude control backup that burns limited propellant with no margin for wheel failures.

what_happened: Before a planned burn to move Juno into a shorter orbit around Jupiter, two helium check valves opened more slowly than expected. NASA postponed the burn and then canceled it.
root_cause: Helium check valves in the fuel pressurization system behaved sluggishly, which made a long engine burn too risky.
what_nasa_did: After a months long investigation, NASA announced on February 17, 2017 that Juno would stay in its 53 day orbit. The longer orbit gave fewer close passes, but it also kept the craft out of the worst radiation.
lesson: When a key valve acts oddly, avoid the one burn that depends on it and redesign the plan.
design_trigger: A critical engine burn that depends on pressurization valves that cannot be retested in flight.

what_happened: Ten days before the Pluto flyby, the main computer was overloaded and the spacecraft went into safe mode. It switched to its backup computer and contact was lost briefly.
root_cause: A timing conflict in the command sequence overloaded the main computer.
what_nasa_did: The team found no hardware or software fault, sent the spacecraft back to normal operations and resumed science on July 7. About 30 observations were lost, less than 1 percent of the science planned for that period.
lesson: Test command sequences for timing overloads, and keep a backup computer that can take over.
design_trigger: A busy command schedule near a one time encounter, with no margin in computer workload.

what_happened: By late 2014 MESSENGER had used most of its propellant and was heading for the surface of Mercury. The team vented the helium that pressurized its fuel tanks through its thrusters to keep it in orbit a little longer.
root_cause: The mission ran low on propellant, and thrusters not built for gas were used with the helium pressurant.
what_nasa_did: Engineers used helium as a cold gas propellant, the first time this was done through hydrazine thrusters, to delay the end. The craft impacted Mercury on April 30, 2015 as planned.
lesson: Look for a second use of leftover resources, such as pressurant gas, when margins run out.
design_trigger: Propellant budget with no reserve and no secondary use of onboard gas.

what_happened: Mars Observer was lost on August 21, 1993, three days before it was to enter orbit around Mars. No one could say for certain why.
root_cause: The board judged a major failure on the pressurization side of the propulsion system most probable, possibly from oxidizer leaking through check valves during the long cruise, but it found no single proven cause.
what_nasa_did: A review board examined 60 failure scenarios and published a final report ranking the most probable causes. It also ranked an electrical power fault and a computer fault as other possible causes.
lesson: Parts built for short use can fail slowly over a long cruise, so qualify and test them for the whole journey.
design_trigger: Check valves and pressurization lines designed for a short use but exposed to a long interplanetary cruise.

what_happened: After a solid rocket motor burn on August 15, 2002, NASA could not make contact with CONTOUR again. There was no data from during the burn.
root_cause: The most probable cause was heat from the motor exhaust plume damaging the spacecraft, but the board could not confirm it because no telemetry or view of the burn existed.
what_nasa_did: A Mishap Investigation Board chaired by NASA's chief engineer listed the plume heating as most probable and catastrophic motor failure, debris and loss of control as alternatives. Its report noted the mission had no telemetry during the burn.
lesson: Always record data during the single most dangerous event, so a failure can be explained.
design_trigger: A one shot solid motor burn with no telemetry coverage and no thermal check of plume heating.

what_happened: Lewis launched on August 23, 1997, and over the next three days its attitude control failed. It went into a flat spin, could not charge its batteries, and contact was lost on August 26.
root_cause: A technically flawed safe mode in the attitude control system, adapted from an earlier mission, plus weak monitoring by the operations team.
what_nasa_did: A Mission Failure Investigation Board found the safe mode design flaw and the team's reliance on it as unproven, along with poor monitoring during early operations. NASA recorded several lessons from the report.
lesson: Prove a safe mode works on the real spacecraft and monitor health closely in the first days.
design_trigger: A reused attitude control design whose safe mode was never tested for thruster imbalance.

what_happened: Soon after launch, the telescope cover blew off early and exposed the frozen hydrogen that kept the detectors cold. The hydrogen boiled away within 48 hours and the spacecraft began to spin.
root_cause: The electronics box that fires the cover explosives had a startup glitch that fired them when it was powered on, because there was no lockout.
what_nasa_did: A Mishap Investigation Board found no component failure, only a design flaw and a missing peer review of the electronics. NASA issued a Parts Advisory to engineers about the startup behavior of electronic devices.
lesson: Design explosive firing circuits with independent inhibits and review how electronics behave at power on.
design_trigger: A pyrotechnic release controlled by programmable electronics with no independent lockout.

what_happened: DART was meant to approach a target satellite on its own, but it bumped into it and was retired early. It used up its thruster fuel after bad navigation data.
root_cause: Navigation software trusted incorrect position and speed data, which caused excess thruster firing and a collision avoidance system without accurate information.
what_nasa_did: A Mishap Investigation Board found no single cause and said several malfunctions in navigation, propellant management and collision avoidance had to occur together. NASA released a 10 page public summary because the full report was restricted.
lesson: Do not let autonomous software trust one sensor, and check its fuel use against the data it relies on.
design_trigger: Autonomous approach logic that trusts a single estimated position with no sanity check or fuel limit.

sources.title: NASA: DART mishap overview
Phys.org: NASA releases DART accident report summary

what_happened: After a routine solar panel adjustment on November 2, 2006, Mars Global Surveyor reported alarms and went silent. Its batteries likely ran down within about 11 hours.
root_cause: A June memory load wrote to wrong addresses, which later drove a solar array into a stop and left the craft at an attitude that overheated a battery.
what_nasa_did: An independent board found the team followed procedures, but the procedures were not enough. It recommended reviewing all non routine uploads and checking contingency modes for overheating risk.
lesson: Review every unusual command upload and make sure safe modes cannot point a battery at the Sun.
design_trigger: Fault protection that can leave a battery or radiator pointed at heat with no thermal check.

what_happened: One of the two solar wings did not fully deploy after launch in November 1996. Engineers suspected a broken damper arm in the deployment mechanism.
root_cause: A part in the solar panel deployment mechanism, suspected to be a damper arm, broke, so one wing did not latch fully open.
what_nasa_did: Managers chose not to force the array to latch and redesigned the aerobraking plan to put less pressure on the panel. Aerobraking was stretched to about a year and mapping began in April 1999.
lesson: When a deployable partly fails, adapt the mission plan instead of forcing the mechanism.
design_trigger: Solar wings that must carry aerobraking loads after a mechanism that has no spare.

what_happened: After launch, Hubble's images were blurry because its main mirror had been ground to the wrong shape. It was perfectly smooth but not the right curve.
root_cause: A test device called the reflective null corrector was assembled with a lens at the wrong spacing, and no other test was trusted over it.
what_nasa_did: The Allen report blamed both the contractor and NASA for weak quality control. NASA built the corrective optics package COSTAR, installed in 1993.
lesson: Never rely on a single test of a critical part, and listen to other tests that disagree.
design_trigger: A critical optic verified by only one test with no end to end check of the finished system.

what_happened: During routine gyro maintenance on June 24 to 25, 1998, ground controllers lost contact with SOHO. The spacecraft lost its pointing, power and thermal control.
root_cause: Ground errors in procedures, a skipped check of the spin status of a gyro and a decision that disabled part of the onboard fault detection.
what_nasa_did: A joint ESA and NASA board found the spacecraft itself was not at fault. Contact returned on August 3, 1998 and SOHO was fully operational by September 25.
lesson: Follow written procedures, control changes to them, and never disable onboard fault protection to save time.
design_trigger: Onboard fault detection that ground commands can turn off during a busy, understaffed operation.

what_happened: Phobos Grunt reached Earth orbit but never left it to go to Mars. Its computer rebooted and put the probe into standby.
root_cause: Space radiation hit memory chips in the computer, and the commission said many chips were not rated for spaceflight. A later report described a software fault that restarted two computer channels.
what_nasa_did: This was a Russian mission, so there was no NASA decision. The Russian commission ruled out outside interference and blamed the use of chips not qualified for space.
lesson: Use space qualified electronics and test the full reboot path on the ground.
design_trigger: Commercial grade chips in a flight computer with no radiation or reboot protection.

what_happened: Beresheet crashed on the Moon on April 11, 2019 during its landing. Its main engine shut down at a bad moment and it did not slow down enough.
root_cause: A gyroscope problem led controllers to send a command that restarted the computer, and the engine shut down in the chain that followed.
what_nasa_did: This was not a NASA mission. SpaceIL's own investigation traced the crash to the ground command and several malfunctions, and the team said it would try again.
lesson: Think hard before sending a manual command during a critical landing, and test what a computer restart does.
design_trigger: A landing that depends on one inertial sensor and allows a ground command to restart the computer mid descent.

what_happened: The lander released its parachute and backshell early and fired its thrusters for only about 3 seconds instead of 30. It crashed on Mars.
root_cause: A motion sensor saturated for about a second after the parachute opened, and the software then computed a negative altitude.
what_nasa_did: This was an ESA mission. An independent board said the flaw was poor handling of sensor saturation and weak parachute modeling, and that the module was very close to landing successfully.
lesson: Design guidance software to handle sensor saturation and test it with real parachute dynamics.
design_trigger: Landing guidance that trusts an inertial sensor reading with no check against the radar altimeter.

what_happened: After a planned maneuver, Hitomi believed it was spinning when it was not. It fired a wheel to stop the phantom spin, started a real spin, and JAXA gave up recovery on April 28, 2016.
root_cause: The attitude control system acted on wrong spin data and wrong control settings, and one measuring device could overrule the others.
what_nasa_did: This was a JAXA mission. JAXA stopped recovery work and published an investigation report in May 2016 on the chain of design, parameter and operations errors.
lesson: Do not let one sensor override all others, and test new control settings against the real deployed structure.
design_trigger: Attitude logic where a single sensor can overrule all others after a configuration change.

what_happened: ICESat's first laser shut down on March 29, 2003 after about 36 days of data. The two later lasers shared the same design.
root_cause: An unexpected failure in a pump diode array, linked to gold and indium parts reacting inside the laser, caused excessive power loss.
what_nasa_did: NASA formed a Tiger Team the next day and an Anomaly Review Board on April 8. The mission moved to roughly 30 day measurement campaigns and resumed with laser 2 in autumn 2003.
lesson: When all copies share a design, one failure mode threatens every spare, so ration their use.
design_trigger: Three identical lasers as backups, so the same hidden failure mode kills them all.

what_happened: NASA last heard from Deep Impact on August 8, 2013 and could not restore contact. After a month of trying, the mission was declared lost.
root_cause: The likely cause was fault protection software that misread dates after August 11, 2013, which caused endless computer reboots.
what_nasa_did: Controllers tried for a month to reach the craft through the Deep Space Network. NASA then declared the mission lost.
lesson: Check that every clock and date in flight software works past its counter limit.
design_trigger: A time counter that overflows during an extended mission and triggers fault protection.

what_happened: On January 21, 2004, Spirit stopped talking to Earth and began rebooting over and over. It could not run tasks that needed its memory.
root_cause: A design error in the file system software and two configuration errors made a large number of stored files crash the computer on startup.
what_nasa_did: Engineers ran the rover without flash memory, deleted thousands of files and reformatted the flash. Spirit returned to normal operations on sol 32.
lesson: Test file systems and memory with the amount of data that will build up over the whole mission.
design_trigger: A flight computer whose file system is large compared with its working memory.

what_happened: A planet wide dust storm blocked the sunlight and Opportunity last spoke to Earth on June 10, 2018. Even after the skies cleared, it stayed silent.
root_cause: The rover depended on sunlight for power, and the dust storm and dust on the panels dropped its voltage too low.
what_nasa_did: Controllers sent more than 835 recovery commands. On February 13, 2019 NASA ended the mission after the last attempt got no reply.
lesson: Solar power systems need margin for long dust storms, and should survive a full battery drain.
design_trigger: A solar powered lander or rover with no way to survive weeks of low sunlight.

what_happened: Dust slowly covered InSight's solar panels, and daily power fell from about 5,000 watt hours at landing to about 500 by May 2022. The team turned off its seismometer to save power and the mission ended in late 2022.
root_cause: The lander had no solar panel cleaning system, and Mars dust built up for years.
what_nasa_did: The team tried scooping soil onto the panel edges to shake dust loose, which helped only partly. NASA planned the wind down as power dropped.
lesson: Plan for dust buildup on solar panels over the full mission, or add a way to clear it.
design_trigger: Solar panels on a dusty world, with no cleaning method, to save weight and power.

what_happened: On February 22, 2022, MAVEN lost contact after a routine power cycle of its main inertial unit. When contact returned, it could not tell which way it was pointing from either of its two units.
root_cause: The inertial measurement units stopped giving usable data, and the second one was also failing.
what_nasa_did: The team finished a star tracker only navigation mode five months early and uplinked it on April 19. MAVEN returned to normal science and relay work on May 28, 2022.
lesson: Build a backup way to find attitude that does not depend on one kind of sensor.
design_trigger: Attitude knowledge that depends on gyro type units with no other sensor as backup.

what_happened: Michael Swartwout's study of university CubeSats found that about 25 percent were dead on arrival in orbit and another 12 percent failed early. Electrical power problems caused nearly half of the failures.
root_cause: Mostly first time teams with weak power systems, computers and radios, with many failures having no known cause.
what_nasa_did: NASA hosted the findings at a 2016 workshop. Swartwout reported that schools with later launches did better, succeeding 75 to 80 percent of the time.
lesson: Test power, deployment and radio end to end, and learn from earlier flights, before the first launch.
design_trigger: A first time team's CubeSat with one power path and a one shot deployed antenna with no tests after full assembly.

what_happened: After landing on Mars, Pathfinder's computer kept resetting itself and losing data. A low priority task held a shared resource that a high priority task needed.
root_cause: Priority inheritance was turned off for a shared lock, so a high priority task missed its deadline and a watchdog reset the computer.
what_nasa_did: JPL repeated the problem on a duplicate unit on Earth in under 18 hours. They then uploaded a short command that switched priority inheritance on.
lesson: Know exactly how commercial software behaves under load and keep a way to patch it in flight.
design_trigger: A real time task schedule sharing a lock between low and high priority tasks.

what_happened: On December 20, 1998, NEAR's first big burn to enter orbit around Eros aborted soon after ignition. The craft then went silent for about 27 hours and used 29 kilograms of fuel.
root_cause: The engine's normal startup surge crossed a sideways acceleration limit set too low, and a command was missing in the abort script.
what_nasa_did: Onboard fault protection brought the craft into a safe sun pointed state. A make up burn on January 3, 1999 moved the rendezvous to February 14, 2000.
lesson: Set safety thresholds from real engine behavior and fully test abort scripts.
design_trigger: A critical engine burn with a safety limit and abort script never tested together.

what_happened: Hours before landing, engineers found that the laser range finders would not fire. Odysseus landed within 1.5 kilometers of its target, tipped over, and one leg broke.
root_cause: A safety switch was left on before launch, so the laser range finders were disabled.
what_nasa_did: The team improvised and used a payload laser sensor to measure distance to the surface hours before landing. The company said the range finders would have worked if the switch had been removed.
lesson: Check every safety lock and enable switch in the launch checklist.
design_trigger: Navigation sensors that need a manual enable step, with no way to flip it in orbit.

what_happened: Soon after launch in October 2021, one of Lucy's two circular solar arrays did not fully open and lock. It was nearly open but not latched.
root_cause: A lanyard that pulls the array open lost tension, wrapped around the motor shaft and came out of its spool.
what_nasa_did: The team ran the main and backup deployment motors together, which pulled in the lanyard and opened the array further. The principal investigator said the mission could fly with the array unlatched.
lesson: Provide backup motors and tension control on any deployable that must open once.
design_trigger: A large deployable solar array pulled open by a single lanyard.

what_happened: On November 13, 2023, Voyager 1 began sending unreadable data. A memory chip in its flight data computer had failed.
root_cause: A memory chip in the Flight Data Subsystem malfunctioned, from either a particle hit or wear after 46 years.
what_nasa_did: JPL engineers sent a command on April 18, 2024 that moved the affected code to a different part of memory. On April 20 engineering data flowed again.
lesson: Keep code relocatable and keep spare memory so a chip failure can be worked around.
design_trigger: A flight computer with no spare memory areas for relocating code after a chip failure.

what_happened: After launch, Peregrine's propulsion system leaked propellant and the lander had no chance of a soft Moon landing. It could not complete its mission.
root_cause: The independent board found the most likely cause was the failure of a helium pressure control valve, called PCV2, possibly from a threaded part loosened by vibration.
what_nasa_did: Astrobotic's review board found the valve failure and shock and vibration tests reproduced the leak on a spare valve. The company redesigned the valve with the vendor and added a regulator and backup latch valves for its next lander.
lesson: Add a regulator and backup valves between the pressurant and the tank, and test valves after vibration.
design_trigger: A single pressure control valve between helium and the oxidizer tank with no backup.

what_happened: On June 4, 1996 the Ariane 5 rocket on its first flight left its course about 40 seconds after liftoff and was destroyed. Its guidance computers had shut down.
root_cause: A number was converted from a larger to a smaller format and overflowed, in code reused from Ariane 4 that had no purpose after liftoff.
what_nasa_did: This was an ESA launch. The Inquiry Board said the failure came from design errors and too little testing, and that unneeded software should not run in flight.
lesson: Do not reuse code without checking that old limits still hold, and do not run unneeded software in flight.
design_trigger: Reused guidance software with unchecked number ranges and no full launch simulation.

what_happened: On February 24, 2009 the Taurus rocket's nose cover did not separate. OCO could not reach orbit and was destroyed.
root_cause: The board could not name one root cause, and four candidates remained, including a frangible joint failure and an electrical or pneumatic fault.
what_nasa_did: A Mishap Investigation Board narrowed 133 fault tree branches to four possible causes. NASA released a public summary in July 2009 because the full report held restricted data.
lesson: Make separation systems fully tested and instrumented, because a stuck nose cover ends a mission.
design_trigger: A launch vehicle separation system with no telemetry for diagnosing a failure.

what_happened: On April 26, 2023, the lander thought it was on the Moon's surface when it was about 5 kilometers up. It ran out of fuel and crashed.
root_cause: Its software treated a correct altitude reading above a crater rim as abnormal and filtered out later readings.
what_nasa_did: This was an ispace mission. The company said its simulations did not model the lunar terrain well and fixed the software for later missions.
lesson: Simulate the real terrain on the approach path and make sensor filters accept real surprises.
design_trigger: Landing software that rejects altitude data that differs from a preset estimate.
